opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that I got into it partly out of curiosity and partly out of a kind of stubbornness. Transformers are incredible, but attention scales quadratically with sequence length, and there's something unsatisfying about the idea that the only way to model long-range dependencies is to have every token look at every other token. State space models come from a very different tradition, from control theory and signal processing, where you have a hidden state that evolves over time and you read outputs off of it. What made them exciting, starting with work like S4 from Albert Gu and colleagues, was showing that if you parameterize that recurrence carefully, you can get something that trains in parallel like a convolution but runs at inference like an RNN, with constant memory per step.

That combination is what I find worth pursuing. You get linear scaling in sequence length, you get fast autoregressive generation without a growing KV cache, and you get a model that's genuinely different in its inductive biases. And then with the selective variants, Mamba and its successors, the gap on language modeling closed a lot more than many people expected.

I don't think the story is "SSMs replace Transformers." I think the more interesting question is what attention is actually buying us, and which parts of it we can get more cheaply. Things like in-context recall and copying still seem to favor attention, and that's why hybrids have become so popular. But having a serious alternative forces us to understand our models better, and that, to me, is the real research value.

r001.rationale: It says SSMs use an evolving hidden state and run like an RNN at inference, but does not identify them as mathematically equivalent to RNNs with linear recurrence.

r002.rationale: It says a carefully parameterized recurrence can train in parallel like a convolution, but does not state that a linear recurrence enables that computation.

r003.rationale: It discusses Transformers’ advantages and the value of alternatives, but does not suggest their cultural entrenchment could impede adoption.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest starting point is that Transformers are great. They work. The attention mechanism gives you this very clean inductive bias where every token can look at every other token, and that turns out to be exactly what you want for a huge range of problems. So I'm not coming at this from a place of thinking Transformers are wrong.

What bothers me is the quadratic cost. Attention scales with the square of the sequence length, and that's not an implementation detail, it's baked into the math. So when people say "we'll just get longer context by throwing more hardware at it," I think they're underestimating how much that constraint shapes what we can actually do. There's a whole class of problems, long documents, audio, genomics, video, agent trajectories that run for hours, where the sequence is just long, and a model that has to keep around and re-read the entire history at every step is fighting against the structure of the problem.

State space models come from a very different lineage. They're essentially recurrent models with a particular structure borrowed from control theory, where you have a fixed-size hidden state that gets updated as you move along the sequence. The thing that made them interesting again, and I'd point to the work from Albert Gu and Chris Ré's group, S4 and then Mamba, is that they found parameterizations where you can train these things in parallel like a convolution, but run them at inference like an RNN. So you get linear time, constant memory per step, and you don't give up the ability to actually train on modern hardware, which was the thing that killed classical RNNs.

From a research perspective, I find that compelling for a few reasons. One is just efficiency, that's the obvious one. But the deeper one is that it forces you to think about what information the model actually needs to carry forward. Attention is a kind of brute-force answer, keep everything and decide later. A state space model has to compress. And compression is where a lot of the interesting questions about what these models are really learning live.

The other thing I'd say is that it's healthy for the field to have a real alternative on the table. For a few years there it felt like architecture research was basically dead, everyone was just scaling the same thing. Having a credible second option, even if it ends up mostly being used in hybrids with attention, which is where I think a lot of the practical systems are heading, makes the whole conversation about what the architecture is doing much sharper. You learn a lot about Transformers by trying to build something that isn't one.

r001.rationale: The response describes state space models as structured recurrent models with a fixed-size hidden state, but does not identify them as mathematically equivalent to RNNs with linear recurrence.

r002.rationale: It says some parameterizations can be trained in parallel like a convolution, but does not explain that linear recurrence enables the convolution-like computation.

r003.rationale: The response says architecture research had focused on scaling Transformers and argues for having an alternative, but does not suggest that Transformers’ cultural entrenchment impedes adoption of alternatives.

astra-6.text:
What I find exciting is that they offer a different tradeoff in how you process a sequence. With a Transformer, you keep representations of the previous tokens around, and attention lets you look back at them. That’s very powerful, but it gets expensive as the sequence gets longer.

A state space model instead maintains a state that it updates as it reads. So you’re compressing the history into something you can carry forward, rather than repeatedly looking back over the whole history. That gives you the possibility of very efficient generation, and, with the right structure, you can still train these models in parallel.

The interesting question is what you lose through that compression. If I ask you to retrieve some specific detail from much earlier in the sequence, attention gives you a fairly direct way to do that. A state space model has to have preserved that information. So I don’t think efficiency alone settles it. What makes this worth pursuing is finding out how much of the capability we associate with Transformers actually requires attention, and how much we can get with a different architecture.

r001.rationale: The response describes a state that updates as it reads, but does not identify state space models as mathematically equivalent to recurrent neural networks with linear recurrence.

r002.rationale: It mentions efficient generation and parallel training, but does not explain that linear recurrence enables convolution-like computation.

r003.rationale: It discusses the tradeoffs of attention and compression, but does not suggest that Transformers’ cultural entrenchment could impede alternative architectures.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find exciting is that they give us a different way to think about memory. In a Transformer, you keep a representation of every token, and attention lets you look back at those representations. That’s very powerful, but the amount of memory and computation grows as the sequence gets longer.

A state space model instead carries forward a state that gets updated as it reads. So there’s a compact memory of what came before. The interesting question is whether you can make that memory expressive enough to do the things we care about, while keeping the efficiency you get from that structure.

And there’s a nice computational aspect: you can formulate these models so they train efficiently in parallel, but at generation time you update them recurrently. That combination is appealing, particularly for long sequences.

I don’t think that means attention goes away. Attention is extremely good at retrieving a particular thing from the past. But it’s worth asking whether every part of a model needs that capability, or whether we can get a better tradeoff with a different architecture, or a combination of the two.

r001.rationale: It says state space models carry and update a state recurrently, but does not identify them as mathematically equivalent to recurrent neural networks with linear recurrence.

r002.rationale: It mentions efficient parallel training, but does not explain convolution-like evaluation enabled by linear recurrence.

r003.rationale: It discusses possible combinations of attention and alternative architectures, but does not suggest that Transformers’ cultural entrenchment could impede adoption.
